records.our_prose: Spinach bolts primarily in response to long days, so the spring window is short: sow as early as the soil can be worked, choose slow-bolting (long-standing) varieties, keep moisture and nitrogen steady, and harvest before the longest days of June. The fall crop, grown under shortening days, rarely bolts and is the main season; overwintered plants bolt in spring as days lengthen, so crop them before the flower stalk elongates.

records.our_prose: Spinach is ready when the leaves are 3 to 6 inches long, dark green, and tender, usually 37 to 50 days from sowing (baby leaf sooner). Harvest the outer leaves cut-and-come-again, or cut the whole rosette about an inch above the crown and let it regrow; pick in the cool morning and crop faster as days lengthen, since the leaves turn bitter once the plant bolts.
source_names: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
records.source_context: Harvest & Storage Spinach should be ready to harvest in about 37 to 45 days after planting. Harvest dark green, tender leaves that are 3 to 6 inches long by picking or cutting individual leaves. Start by picking the outer leaves and then harvest the newer leaves as they reach the desired size.

records.our_prose: A small fly lays eggs on the underside of the leaves, and the maggots that hatch tunnel inside the leaf between the top and bottom layers, eating as they go. Spinach, beets, and chard are its favorites.

records.source_context: The adults can be seen flying near the ground between the plants. The females deposit eggs singly or in rows of two to five side by side on the underside of the leaves. In as little as three days but more commonly in four to six days the tiny legless, white to yellowish maggots hatch from the eggs and work their way into the leaf tissue.

records.our_prose: St. George's Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) grows spinach on two direct-sown cycles, per Utah State University Extension's suggested vegetable planting dates for Utah. The spring sowing runs February 15 to March 1, the Group A (Hardy) date for St. George, with leaves ready in about 45 days and the crop cut by mid-April before it bolts. USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes put St. George over 100°F in June, July, and August, and USU's Group E "Special Plants for Fall Harvest" table does not open the fall spinach window until July 1, so May and June together form a genuine two-month bare-ground pause, the longest of this family's fall-paired crops. Spinach is very cold tolerant, so the fall stand, sown July 1 to August 15, keeps producing well past the November 1 average first frost.
